name: Old Babylonia
title: Social Hierarchy of Old Babylonia: From King to Enslaved
period: c. 1894–1595 BCE (the First Dynasty of Babylon)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are hailed as the shepherd chosen by the gods: you lead the army, hear appeals from your subjects and, when you take the throne, proclaim “justice” by cancelling debts.
tiers.kid: The king of Babylon led the army, built temples and canals, and had his laws carved on a tall stone.
tiers.rise: The throne stayed in one Amorite family for three centuries and normally passed from father to son: Hammurabi succeeded his father Sin-muballit in 1792 BCE, and his son Samsu-iluna succeeded him.
tiers.why: The king of Babylon ruled as the servant chosen by the gods.

tiers.name: Royal officials
tiers.you: You serve the king as a governor or minister, answering his letters about canals, taxes and lawsuits, and you hold your fields only for as long as you serve him.
tiers.kid: Officials helped the king run his kingdom, looking after canals, taxes and court cases.
tiers.rise: Office depended on the king’s favour: a secretary such as Sin-iddinam could rise to govern a province, and during the war with Elam Hammurabi brought three officials of a rival court, Ekallatum, into his council.
tiers.why: Hammurabi governed through a small circle of men bound to him personally.

tiers.name: Priests and nadītu
tiers.you: Your family dedicated you to the sun god, and you live in the walled cloister at Sippar; you may not marry, but you lease out your fields and lend silver in your own name.
tiers.kid: Priests cared for the temples of the gods, and some women, called nadītu, lived together in a walled cloister.
tiers.rise: Priestly offices passed within families or were bought; a girl became a nadītu when her family dedicated her and guaranteed her keep, and what she owned went back to her family when she died.
tiers.why: Each city’s great temple was the household of its god, run by a chief administrator (šangûm) and served by priests of many kinds: some fed and clothed the god’s statue, others sang laments to calm the gods, and…

tiers.name: Scribes
tiers.you: You spent your boyhood copying signs, word lists and Sumerian proverbs in your teacher’s house; now you write the contracts, letters and receipts of the palace, the temples and the merchants.
tiers.kid: Scribes wrote letters, contracts and laws by pressing wedge-shaped marks into soft clay.
tiers.rise: Writing opened the way into the king’s service: Hammurabi’s secretaries handled state secrets, and one of them, Sin-iddinam, became governor of Larsa.
tiers.why: Scribes wrote the contracts, letters, receipts and court records on which Babylonian life ran, pressing wedge-shaped signs into clay.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You lend silver and grain at interest, send agents out with your capital and buy copper shipped from Dilmun; the Code limits the interest you may charge.
tiers.kid: Merchants bought and sold goods such as copper, and lent silver and grain to people who needed them.
tiers.rise: Trading and lending were open to anyone with silver, and temples and nadītu lent at interest too; credit could fail, and part of Ea-nasir’s house was later joined to a neighbour’s, perhaps after his fortunes fell.
tiers.why: Merchants (tamkārum) were the traders and bankers of Babylonia.

tiers.name: Soldiers on service land
tiers.you: You hold a field, an orchard and a house from the king, and when he calls a campaign you must march; your land cannot be sold or taken for your debts, and if you are captured your son will take over your service.
tiers.kid: Soldiers were given land by the king, and in return they had to fight whenever he called them.
tiers.rise: Service land passed to a son who could do the service, so soldiering often ran in families; a man who failed to serve, or left his field, lost it to another who did.
tiers.why: The king’s soldiers held land from the crown in return for service, the obligation called ilkum.

tiers.name: Free men and their families
tiers.you: You farm barley and dates on the family plot or on rented land; the law repays any injury to you in kind, but one flood or drought can put your family in debt.
tiers.kid: Most free Babylonians were farmers who grew barley and dates in fields watered by canals.
tiers.rise: A family that prospered could buy land, lend at interest or win a service field; one that fell into debt could lose its land or have to send a wife, son or daughter into debt service.
tiers.why: The awīlum, literally “man”, was the free man of full standing in the Code of Hammurabi, and his household was the basic unit of Babylonian society.

tiers.name: Commoners (muškēnū)
tiers.you: You are free and may own a field and even a slave, but the law counts you for less than an awīlum: whoever blinds you pays silver instead of losing his own eye.
tiers.kid: The laws treated muškēnū as free people, but of lower rank than the full free men called awīlū.
tiers.rise: How a family came to be counted among the muškēnū, or rose out of them, is not known.
tiers.why: The muškēnum stood between the full free man and the slave, and who he was is still debated.

tiers.name: Slaves
tiers.you: You belong to another household, which can sell you, pledge you for its debts or give you away with a dowry; your hairlock marks you as a slave, and anyone who shelters you if you run away risks death.
tiers.kid: Slaves were owned by other people and had to work without pay, though some were set free.
tiers.rise: Owners could free slaves, often by adopting them, as nadītu at Sippar did with the women they made their heirs; family members bound for debt went free after three years or when a king proclaimed a release.
tiers.why: Slaves (wardum, amtum) were property: they could be sold, pledged for debt, given as part of a dowry and inherited, and they wore a distinctive hairlock (abbuttum) that no barber might shave off without the owner’s…
